source.title: Understanding the Double Descent Phenomenon in Deep Learning

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives test-risk formulas for linear regression as model capacity changes. This tests the general double-descent behavior with an analytical method, rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's figures showing deep-network, RFF, and other cited results are attributed to prior work and are not recorded as this study's results. The rows below cover the paper's own risk formulas in Theorem 19 and Corollary 1.
record.test_reason: This is a tutorial or review (a DAC master's project write-up) explaining double descent. It reports no new experiments. Its linear-regression risk formula (Theorem 19 and Corollary 1) restates the known result from Belkin, Hsu & Xu (arXiv:1903.07571): Figure 5a showing this curve is 'Taken from [5]'. The classical regime is attributed to Breiman & Freedman [7], and the key inverse-Wishart step is called 'beyond the scope of this tutorial'. The RFF, deep-network and jamming results are all cited figures. No result of the study's own bears on any version, so the reader's 'tests'/T2 is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The tutorial concludes that double descent arises from well-chosen inductive biases (e.g., minimum-norm solutions selected by gradient descent) in the over-parameterized regime. It says double descent has been studied in linear settings and observed with deep networks, and that its deep-learning mechanisms remain an open question. It points to multiple-descent work (Chen et al.). The authors do not claim to derive the linear results themselves; they present them from prior work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses analytical risk derivations for Gaussian linear regression and feature selection, rather than the original sources' empirical deep-network size, epoch, or data sweeps.
record.problems: The study's own derived results concern specific linear-regression assumptions; its cited deep-network and RFF plots are not new results in this paper. The risk formulas do not test epoch-wise or sample-size double descent.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figures and claims taken from cited works were excluded as instructed.

untested.parts: No own model-size sweep. Deep-network curves (Fig. 2) are taken from Nakkiran et al.
No own epoch-wise measurement. Fig. 2 is cited.
Only restated prior analytical results (linear regression, RFF on MNIST from Belkin et al.); nothing new.
EMC is defined and the hypothesis restated from Nakkiran et al.; not tested.
Multiple descent is mentioned only by citation (Chen et al.); no noise or regularization test.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a tutorial or review whose original contributions are expository proofs of known results: GD converges to the minimum-norm solution, and GD on separable data converges to the SVM direction. Neither is a measurement of double descent. It is not an original source. No verdicts are given because nothing is tested.

versions.untested_parts: No own model-size sweep or test-error result for deep networks.
No own test-error measurement over training epochs.
No test of increasing sample size near a fixed interpolation threshold.
The paper derives results for specific linear-regression settings, not across model classes generally. Its RFF and deep-network curves are cited from other work.
EMC is defined and discussed, but no test compares peak locations across axes using a single effective-complexity measure.
No comparison tests whether noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
No test measures the curve against an effective parameter count to assess whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: linear regression class H_p
rows.size_stated: p non-zero components; d total components
rows.operation_detail: Analytically evaluates test risk as the number p of selected features changes.

conditions.value: X has independent standard Gaussian entries; response is defined using Gaussian noise with variance σ².
X is assumed full row rank and n ≪ d.
ERM in H_p, using the minimum Euclidean norm solution.

rows.measure: Expected squared test risk E[(y − xᵀŵ)²] as a function of p.
rows.value: Theorem 19 gives (||w_∼q||² + σ²)(1 + p/(n−p−1)) if p ≤ n−2; +∞ if n−1 ≤ p ≤ n+1; and ||w_∼p||²(1 − n/p) + (||w_∼q||² + σ²)(1 + n/(p−n−1)) if p ≥ n+2.
rows.note: The formula has a risk divergence around the interpolation region and finite risk on the over-parameterized side, where the terms involving p−n−1 decrease as p grows.
rows.check: Cited result, not the study's own. Theorem 19 restates Belkin, Hsu & Xu (2019) 'Two models of double descent for weak features'. The paper's plot of it (Fig. 5a) is 'Taken from [5]', and the proof is only sketched, deferring the hard term. It should not be a row of this study.

rows.subject: linear regression class H_p
rows.operation_detail: Averages the test-risk expression over uniformly random subsets of p features as p changes.

conditions.value: Uniformly random subset T of {1,…,d} with cardinality p.

rows.measure: Expected squared test risk, with expectation also taken over the random feature subset.
rows.value: Corollary 1 gives ((1 − p/d)||w||² + σ²)(1 + p/(n−p−1)) if p ≤ n−2; and ||w||²(1 − n/d(2 − (d−n−1)/(p−n−1))) + σ²(1 + n/(p−n−1)) if p ≥ n+2.
rows.note: The stated formula omits the singular intermediate range n−1 ≤ p ≤ n+1; the corollary gives the averaged risk on the two ranges shown.
rows.check: Cited result. Corollary 1 is the random-feature-subset average from the same prior work (Belkin, Hsu & Xu 2019), reproduced in tutorial form. It is not a new derivation or measurement by this study. The formula transcription is otherwise accurate.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
